title: Comparative constructions
description: Explore scalar and non-scalar comparison, comparative clauses, than/as phrases, non-scalar likeness, and comparative and superlative set comparison.
example: The new bridge is slightly longer than the old one, but it is not as beautiful as the stone bridge upstream.

intro: *The new bridge is slightly longer than the old one* does one kind of work; *it is not as beautiful as the stone bridge upstream* does another. Both are comparisons, and both draw on the same small set of markers, yet one ranks two values on a scale while the other says the new bridge falls short on a different scale. English also compares for identity (*the same bus as last time*) and for likeness (*similar to the old one*), where no scale is involved at all.

The chapter follows two distinctions that cut across each other: scalar versus non-scalar, and equality versus inequality. From there it moves to term and set comparison, to the governors that license comparative clauses, and to the *than*/*as* phrases that carry the secondary term. Later sections take up *as*, *like* and *unlike*, and the comparative and superlative forms that rank a member within a set.

A question worth asking of every example: what is being compared, and on what dimension? A degree, an identity, a likeness, a rank within a group — the syntax can look alike while the interpretation shifts. The sections that follow keep returning to that question.

blocks.text: Take *She is much bigger than she was then*. The word *bigger* carries a grade inflection, and the clause *than she was then* is a comparative clause — one of the three major kinds of finite subordinate clause in English. *She went to the same school as I went to* contains the same kind of subordinate clause, though nothing is being graded.

*Very big*, *quite big* and *rather big* turn the volume up on a property, but they do not bring a second term along. *Bigger than* does: it sets two values against each other on a scale. The two systems overlap in the adjectives they use, and that overlap is exactly what makes them easy to confuse.

*I took the same bus as last time* compares two buses for identity, and *I took a different bus from last time* compares them for difference. Neither ranks anything. They borrow *as* and *than* from the scalar system — *different than* turns up in some varieties — but the question they answer is whether the terms are the same, not how much they differ.

blocks.text: *Kim is as old as Pat* and *Kim is older than Pat* both ask us to place two ages on a scale. The first puts them at the same point or above it; the second puts Kim higher. What makes the comparison scalar is the gradable expression — *old*, *heavy*, *careful* — and the marker says where the terms sit.
*I took the same bus as last time* asks whether the bus is the same one; *I took a different bus from last time* asks whether it is not. Nothing gradable is at stake, and no ranking follows.

*As* marks equality in both types, which is why the parallel is tempting. *Than* marks scalar inequality and some non-scalar inequality, as in *other than* or, in some varieties, *different than*. Sharing a marker is not sharing a meaning: the scalar use locates values, the non-scalar use sorts entities.

blocks.text: In *Ed is more tolerant than he used to be*, two degrees of tolerance are held up against each other: Ed now, Ed then. Call the one in the matrix clause the primary term and the one in the comparative clause the secondary term. The labels matter less than the split, since each term belongs to a different clause layer.

*Ed made the most mistakes of them all* works differently. There is no second term to pair with Ed; instead a set — *them all* — provides the field, and Ed is placed at the top of it. *It sold for the highest price ever paid for a Cézanne* does the same with a set of prices.

The secondary term can go unsaid when context supplies it: *Ed was difficult then, but now he’s more tolerant* leaves *than he was then* to be recovered. Set comparisons often rewrite as term comparisons — *Ed made more mistakes than all the others* — which is a useful check on what the set actually contains.

blocks.text: Something in the matrix has to license the comparison. *More*, *less*, *as*, *so*, *such*, *than*, *superior*, *inferior*, *prefer* and *rather* all do that work; call them comparative governors. What separates them is the complement each one allows: a clause, an NP or a phrase.

The governor and its complement form a comparative phrase. In *much bigger than she was*, *much* modifies *bigger* and *than she was* completes it; in *as careful as her sister*, the phrase is *as careful* and the complement is *as her sister*. The modifier sits inside the phrase, the complement outside the head.

Treating *than* and *as* as prepositions rather than subordinating conjunctions changes where the clause sits: it becomes the complement of the preposition. That analysis survives reduction. *Bob is as generous as Sue* has a one-word complement, and the missing material — *as Sue is generous* — is recovered from the matrix rather than spelled out.

blocks.text: *She is much bigger than she was then* leaves us to supply the complement of *was*: we hear it as *big*. That gap is not sloppiness. The clause borrows structure from the matrix, which is why the comparison can be reduced and still understood.

Reduction has limits. *She wrote more plays than he wrote novels* is fine with the measure after *more* left empty. Put the measure in — *She wrote more plays than he wrote five novels* — and the sentence collapses. The comparative clause cannot spell out the very quantity that the comparison is measuring.

Reduction can go further, down to one remnant: *Bob is as generous as Sue*, *She is taller than him*. That remnant identifies the secondary term, and everything else comes from the matrix. Which element survives is decided by what the comparison needs to pick out.

blocks.text: The remnant after *than* or *as* is usually an NP or a pronoun. *Bob is as generous as Sue* and *She is taller than him* each supply just enough to identify the second term, while the rest of the clause is understood.

*She is taller than I* and *She is taller than me* identify the same secondary term, but they wear their clause structure differently. Formal writing favours the nominative when a subject is understood; informal speech uses the accusative. The nominative makes the clausal source more visible.

The remnant can also be a phrase: *more quickly than before*, *as often as ever*. *Than before* is read as *than she was before*, *as ever* as *as she ever was*. The governor and the matrix decide what the fragment is understood to contain.

sections.title: Likeness, contrast, and the comparative phrase

blocks.text: Comparison does not always set values against each other. *She looks like her mother* asserts likeness; *She looks different from her mother* asserts contrast. The complement can be an NP, a PP or a clause depending on the governor — *like her mother*, *different from her mother*, *the same as her mother*.

*More apparent than real* is stranger than it looks. Nothing is more apparent than something else; the sentence measures how well the description *apparent* fits against the description *real*. The syntax is comparative, but the comparison is between labels, not between degrees of a property.

*More apparent than real* sounds fine; *more apparent than the surface* does not. The reduced clause has to match the matrix category by category and function by function. A poor match leaves the comparison odd or ambiguous, which is why a sentence can be grammatical and still hard to read.

sections.title: Scalar inequality: more, less, and superior

blocks.text: Scalar inequality comes in two directions. *Bigger than* and *more careful than* mark superiority; *less big than* and *less careful than* mark inferiority. Only superiority has an inflectional form. Equality and inferiority are built with separate words.

*Older than* and *younger than* are both superiority comparatives: each says the primary term is further along its scale. The scales run opposite ways, so *younger* moves towards zero while *older* moves away from it. Superiority is a grammatical relation, not a compass direction.

*More* and *less* also quantify nouns and combine with degree determinatives: *more mistakes*, *fewer mistakes*, *less money*, *much more useful*. *Rather*, *prefer*, *superior* and *inferior* are peripheral governors with their own complements — *prefer tea to coffee*, *superior to the old model* — and they select *to* rather than *than*.

sections.title: Scalar equality: as, so, and such

blocks.text: *Kim is as old as Pat* is true if Kim is older; it only rules out Kim being younger. Equality is usually a floor, not an exact match. Negate it — *Kim isn’t as old as Pat* — and the floor disappears, leaving inferiority.

Why the lower-bound reading? Most scales resist precise measurement, so exact equality is rarely the issue. *He made as many as eighteen mistakes* leans towards exactness because the number is explicit; *He made as many mistakes as I did* does not.

*So* and *such* handle neighbouring jobs: *so careful as to check twice*, *such a careful worker as Pat*. *As* is the general equality marker across scalar and non-scalar comparison, while *so* is more restricted and usually pulls a result or degree clause along with it.

blocks.text: Degree modifiers adjust the gap between the two terms: *much bigger*, *far more useful*, *slightly less expensive*, *rather better*. *Very* is the odd one out — *very bigger* fails, though *very much bigger* works, because *very* modifies the adjective rather than the comparative.

*The* can attach to a comparative and turn it into a selector: *the bigger of the two*, *the more useful option*. It picks one alternative out of two, or one member out of a small set. That is close to superlative work but stops short of ranking an entire set.

The correlative comparative pairs two of these phrases: *The more you practise, the better you become*. The first sets a degree or condition, the second reports what varies with it. *The sooner, the better* is the same construction with both halves trimmed.

blocks.text: The non-scalar family sorts into three relations. *Same* claims identity, or at least exact correspondence; *similar* claims likeness without identity; *different* claims non-identity. The examples below show how little the nouns matter: a bus, a design, a person. None of these comparisons ranks anything.

Each governor brings its own complement pattern: *same as*, *similar to*, *different from*, *different than* in some varieties, *other than*, *else*. *Like* takes an NP and expresses likeness; *unlike* expresses contrast. None of these ranks two values, even when *as* or *than* appears.

*Such* compares kind or quality — *such a report as this*, *such reports as these*. *Other* and *else* mark difference or exclusion — *someone other than Kim*, *nothing else*. The governor dictates what can follow it, and the relation follows the governor.

blocks.text: *As* is the busiest of the markers. It carries scalar equality in *as old as*, non-scalar identity in *the same as*, and exemplification in *such as*. Its complement may be a clause or a reduced phrase, which is one reason it spreads across so many constructions.

*Like* is a preposition of likeness — *She looks like her mother* — but it also takes finite clauses in some constructions: *It looks like it’s going to rain*. *As* can introduce a comparison or a supplement: *As you know, the deadline is Friday*. Its territory is wider than equality alone.

*Unlike* is not merely *not like*. It sets the subject against the complement, often in a detached supplement: *Unlike her sister, she stayed calm*. The relation is contrast between entities, not a position on a scale.

sections.title: Scalar set comparison: comparative and superlative

blocks.text: Set comparison needs a set. With two members, the comparative does the work: *the bigger of the two*. With more, the superlative picks out the extreme: *the biggest of the three*, *the most useful option*.

*Biggest* and *most useful* both mark the extreme of a set, but they do it by different means: one inflects, the other uses *most*. And *most* has a second life meaning “very” in *a most interesting article*. Context separates the absolute reading, which intensifies, from the relative reading, which ranks.

The set can be spelled out with *of* or *in* — *the best of the three*, *the tallest in the class* — or left to context, as in *She is the tallest*. Relative superlatives normally take *the*, the definite article anchoring the ranking.

blocks.text: Two distinctions organise everything in this chapter: scalar versus non-scalar, and equality versus inequality. Scalar comparison places values on a scale; non-scalar comparison asks about identity, likeness or difference. Cutting across them is the difference between term comparison, which pairs a primary and a secondary term, and set comparison, which ranks a member within a group.

Comparative governors decide what kind of complement appears. *Than* and *as* take clauses or reduced phrases, and those clauses are incomplete by design. Superiority may be inflectional or analytic; inferiority and equality are analytic. Scalar equality sets a lower bound rather than an exact value.

*Same*, *similar*, *different*, *other*, *else*, *as*, *like* and *unlike* cover the non-scalar ground, while comparative and superlative forms handle sets, with *most* split between absolute and relative readings. Because the markers recur across types, the construction and the context have to settle what is being compared.

blocks.title: A comparison checklist
blocks.text: Identify the primary term and the secondary term or set. Decide whether the comparison is scalar or non-scalar, equality or inequality. Find the governor and its complement. Then check whether the clause is reduced and whether the reading is metalinguistic, absolute or relative.

check.prompt: Which statement correctly describes scalar equality?

options.text: It normally means “at least equal” and excludes inferiority.
options.feedback: It is compatible with superiority unless context suggests exact equality.
Than marks inequality; as marks equality.

worked: Take *The new bridge is slightly longer than the old one, but it is not as beautiful as the stone bridge upstream*. The first comparison is scalar inequality: *longer than* expresses superiority on the length scale, modified by *slightly*. The secondary term is *the old one*.

The second comparison is scalar equality under negation: *not as beautiful as the stone bridge upstream* entails that the new bridge is less beautiful. The comparison set is the two bridges, and the scale is beauty. The example contrasts superiority and inferiority using the same comparative system.
application: Find the governor: more, less, as, than, same, similar, different, like or a superlative. Identify the primary term and the secondary term or set. Then decide whether the comparison is scalar or non-scalar and whether it expresses equality or inequality.

For a comparative clause, reconstruct the omitted material from the matrix. Check whether the reduction is to a single element, a phrase or a full clause. Then identify the function of the gap or remnant inside the comparative clause.

For a superlative, identify the comparison set and decide whether the reading is relative or absolute. For non-scalar comparison, decide whether the relation is identity, likeness, difference or exclusion. The markers overlap, but the interpretations do not.
reveal: In *The new bridge is slightly longer than the old one, but it is not as beautiful as the stone bridge upstream*, *longer than* is a scalar superiority comparison and *not as beautiful as* is a negated scalar equality entailing inferiority. The secondary terms are *the old one* and *the stone bridge upstream*.
recap: Scalar comparison ranks values on a scale; non-scalar comparison concerns identity, likeness and difference. Term comparison relates two terms; set comparison ranks a member within a set. Comparative clauses are reduced and interpreted through the matrix.

More, less, as, than, same, similar, different, like and unlike are comparative governors with different complement patterns. Scalar equality gives a lower bound, and superlatives can be relative or absolute.
